meta.title: THE FIRST 90 DAYS
meta.subtitle: YOU GOT THE JOB. NOW MEET THE JOB.
meta.researchNote: An illustrated synthesis of interview themes—not a day-by-day diary of a real participant.
meta.composite: Illustrative composite. Names, briefs, comments and messages are invented for this exhibit.
meta.notLongitudinal: These are narrative turning points, not observations of one person over time.

how: Turn a page with the corner tab, the arrow keys or a swipe.
Things on the desk move too: the mug, the badge, the sketchbook, the pencil.
Every day has two sides. Switch between the new designer and the team.

days.headline: CONGRATULATIONS. YOU’RE IN.
days.student: The letter says yes. It says when to arrive and what the job is called. It doesn’t say what Monday looks like.
days.team: For the team, the hire is one line on a busy list. They’re already planning what you’ll pick up first, and assume you know more than you do.
days.slip: A job title arrived before the job did.
days.mug: What should I have ready for my first morning?
days.basis: Day theme from the Studio Bridge interview synthesis: the gap between accepting an offer and knowing what the work involves.

letter.body: We’re delighted to offer you the position of Junior Designer. You’ll start on Monday at 9:30 and report to the Design Lead. Please bring your ID.

margin: Bring a laptop? A portfolio? Lunch?

print.prompt: Write down three things the letter didn’t tell you.

days.headline: HELLO, EVERYONE.
days.student: Twelve names before lunch. The org chart shows who reports to whom. It doesn’t show who actually knows where things are.
days.team: Everyone remembers their own first day. Few remember to explain the things they now do without thinking.
days.slip: The chart showed reporting lines, not how things actually get done.
days.mug: Who should I go to when I’m stuck, and is that the same person who reviews my work?
days.basis: Bauer (2010, p. 2) separates formal and informal norms (“culture”) and the relationships a newcomer needs (“connection”). The chart and its unwritten version are invented.

nodes.name: Studio Head
nodes.unwritten: Signs off on anything that goes to a new client.

nodes.name: Account Manager
nodes.unwritten: Knows what the client actually cares about.

nodes.name: Senior Designer
nodes.unwritten: Knows where the brand files really live.

nodes.name: You
nodes.unwritten: Nobody has told you lunch is at 1:15. Everyone goes.

nodes.name: Producer
nodes.unwritten: Knows which deadlines are real deadlines.

print.prompt: Draw the chart you were given. Then draw who you actually ask.

days.headline: THAT’S IN MY JOB DESCRIPTION?
days.student: The description said “create engaging visual content”. This week that meant resizing, renaming, exporting, and one sketch you were proud of.
days.team: Production work keeps a studio running. Someone has to do it, and it’s often how a newcomer learns the systems.
days.slip: Most of the week was in the description, just in vaguer words.
days.mug: What does a normal week look like for the person who did this before me?
days.basis: Bauer (2010, p. 5): role clarity, how well a newcomer understands the role and its expectations, is one of the main adjustment outcomes. The job description and tasks are invented.

interaction.jd: Junior Designer: create engaging visual content across print and digital; support the team on brand projects; collaborate with stakeholders.
tasks: Resize one banner into nine formats
Rename 140 files to the naming convention
Update last year’s deck with new numbers
Export print-ready PDFs for the printer
Sit in on a client call (mic off)
Sketch three ideas for a logo refresh
interaction.after: There’s no answer key. Most of it fits under “support the team”. That phrase is doing a lot of work.

print.prompt: List this week’s tasks. Tick the ones the job description named.

days.headline: THREE COMMENTS. ONE FILE.
days.student: Three people opened the same file and left three different notes. They can’t all go first.
days.team: Each reviewer is looking after something different: the brand, the client, the deadline. Nobody thinks they’re contradicting anyone.
days.slip: Conflicting notes often meant different responsibilities, not different opinions of me.
days.mug: When comments conflict, who makes the final call?
days.basis: Bauer (2010, p. 5) notes that ambiguous expectations get in the way of performance. The three comments are invented.

comments.text: The logo needs more breathing room.
Client wants the price much bigger.
The type hierarchy is fighting itself.

interaction.after: There isn’t one right order. A useful reply might be: “A bigger price will crowd the logo. Which matters more for Thursday?”

print.prompt: Three comments, one file. Number them, then write the question you’d ask.

days.headline: IS THIS A STUPID QUESTION?
days.student: The draft has been open since 10:40. It starts with “Sorry, probably obvious, but…”
days.team: The team would rather answer a question now than redo the job on Friday. Most of them can’t remember who asked what.
days.slip: Asking felt like exposing a gap. Not asking left the gap in the work.
days.mug: Is there a good time of day for quick questions?
days.basis: Bauer (2010, p. 13) describes information-seeking and feedback-seeking as proactive behaviours that help newcomers adjust, and notes some hesitate to ask for fear of exposing weaknesses. The draft and reply are invented.

interaction.draft: Sorry to bother you!! Quick question, probably really obvious, but
interaction.rewrite: Before I export: does the printer need CMYK or RGB?

options.send: Sent. Reply, two minutes later: “CMYK. Good catch.”
options.keep: Still in drafts. The question is still there, and so is the export.
options.rewrite: Shorter. No apology. The question is the whole message now.

print.prompt: Write the question you’ve been putting off. Cross out the apology.

days.headline: SMALL CHANGE. BIG RIPPLE.
days.student: One line changed in the brief. By the afternoon it had touched every file.
days.team: Briefs change because clients learn things too. Part of the job is spotting what a change touches.
days.slip: A brief is a draft too. The job includes noticing what a change touches.
days.mug: When the brief changes, can the deadline change with it?
days.basis: Role clarity (Bauer 2010, p. 5) is not fixed at the start; a revised brief resets part of it. The brief is invented.

interaction.verb: Slide the revised brief over the original
ripple: The photography no longer fits the audience
The reel needs motion time nobody scheduled

print.prompt: Original brief / revised brief. List what the change touches.

days.headline: AM I LEARNING OR JUST DOING?
days.student: A month of being busy. Is busy the same as learning?
days.team: From the outside, a newcomer doing lots of tasks looks like progress. Whether it feels like growth is harder to see.
days.slip: Doing and learning overlapped, but not completely.
days.mug: Which of my tasks are meant to teach me something, and which just need doing?
days.basis: Deloitte’s 2025 Gen Z and Millennial Survey found learning and development among the top three reasons for choosing an employer. The checklist is invented; your answers aren’t scored.

items: Sat in on two client calls
Presented one idea in the crit
interaction.after: Anything marked “Learned something” goes onto the Day 45 agenda.

print.prompt: What did you do this month? Circle what taught you something.

days.headline: WE NEED TO TALK.
days.student: A calendar invite titled “Check-in”. No description. Your stomach reads it as “we need to talk”.
days.team: Most check-ins are routine. Without an agenda, a newcomer fills the gap with the worst case.
days.slip: The talk was a check-in. An agenda made it a conversation.
days.mug: Could check-ins come with an agenda?
days.basis: Bauer (2010, p. 13) lists feedback-seeking among the behaviours that help newcomers adjust. The agenda is invented.

interaction.title: Check-in · 30 min

items.d: Priorities, who signs off, what “done” means here.
One thing to keep doing, one to change, from each of you.

items.h: What I’d like to learn next

items.d: One piece of work to own end to end.

interaction.empty: Nothing carried over from Day 30 yet. Turn back and mark what you learned from.

print.prompt: Write the agenda you’d want for your first check-in.

days.headline: NOT EVERYTHING SHOWS UP IN A PORTFOLIO.
days.student: Two months of work. One poster you could show anyone. The rest made other people’s work easier.
days.team: The team noticed who fixed the shared styles and who took the notes. None of that will be in a portfolio.
days.slip: A lot of the work was invisible in the files and visible in how the team worked.
days.mug: How does shared, behind-the-scenes work get recognised here?
days.basis: Bauer (2010, p. 5) names social integration, feeling accepted and connected with colleagues, as an adjustment outcome. The tasks are invented.

items: Took the notes in client calls
Caught a wrong date before print
Showed the intern where the brand files live
Kept the job sheet up to date
interaction.after: Most of this is evidence of collaboration. It turns up in references and the next project, not on a portfolio page.

print.prompt: Two columns: what you could show, and what the team would remember.

days.headline: DO I LIKE THE WORK, OR JUST THE IDEA OF IT?
days.student: You wanted brand design. You like the systems part more than the big reveal. That’s new.
days.team: The team is learning where you’re strongest too. A preference is useful information, not disloyalty.
days.slip: Some preferences held. Some changed once the work was real.
days.mug: Can I try more of the work I’ve found I like?
days.basis: Day theme from the Studio Bridge interview synthesis: preferences change once the work is real. The lists are invented; nothing you pick is scored.

interaction.verb: Lay the tabs over each other

print.prompt: The idea of the job / the work as it is / what you’d keep.

days.headline: WHAT HAVE WE LEARNED ABOUT EACH OTHER?
days.student: Not a review. Two lists side by side, and one place where they overlap.
days.team: The team has been adjusting too: to how you work, what you need, and what you’re good at.
days.mug: What would you like me to do more of in the next 90 days?
days.basis: Bauer (2010, p. 2) frames onboarding as something the organisation does too (clarification, culture, connection), not just the newcomer. The lists are invented.

a.title: What I learned about the team
items: They decide fast and revise often
Fridays are for sending, not starting

b.title: What the team learned about me
items: Needs the why behind a change

interaction.overlap: Show work in progress. Ask early.

print.prompt: Two lists. Where do they overlap?

days.headline: THE FIRST JOB WAS NEVER ONE MOMENT.
days.student: Ninety days on, nobody mentions the offer letter. What’s left is a long run of small days.
days.team: From the team’s side, the hire also became real gradually, through the work.
days.slip: Understanding arrived in pieces, after the offer.
days.mug: What should the next 90 days be about?
days.basis: Onboarding guidance often treats about 90 days as the window to prove yourself (Bauer 2010, p. 1). This calendar suggests understanding keeps accumulating rather than arriving on a deadline.

print.prompt: Mark the days that changed how you saw the job.

badge.gets: The building, the Wi-Fi, the shared drive

finding.headline: THE OFFER WAS DAY ZERO. THE UNDERSTANDING CAME LATER.
finding.intro: Three threads ran through the calendar. Nothing here is measured or scored; these are the things the pages noticed, plus anything you added.
finding.close: A job offer is a beginning, not a description.

sb.title: Studio Bridge primary research: thematic synthesis
sb.note: Interviews with students, educators, design professionals and employers. The twelve day themes come from that synthesis as set out in the exhibition brief. Paraphrased; no participant is quoted, and no individual was followed over 90 days.

bauer2010.title: Onboarding New Employees: Maximizing Success
bauer2010.publisher: Talya N. Bauer, SHRM Foundation Effective Practice Guidelines, 2010
bauer2010.note: The “Four C’s” (compliance, clarification, culture, connection; p. 2); newcomer adjustment through self-efficacy, role clarity, social integration and knowledge of culture (pp. 4–6); information- and feedback-seeking as proactive behaviours, and reluctance to ask questions that might reveal one’s weaknesses (p. 13); about 90 days to prove yourself (p. 1).

deloitte2025.title: 2025 Gen Z and Millennial Survey
deloitte2025.note: Over 23,000 respondents in 44 countries. Learning and development ranked among the top three reasons for choosing a current employer.

disclaimers: An illustrated synthesis of interview themes—not a day-by-day diary of a real participant.
The twelve days are narrative turning points, not longitudinal data. Nobody was followed for 90 days.
Names, roles, letters, briefs, comments, drafts and replies are invented composites.
No interview quotations appear here; themes are paraphrased.
Nothing is scored. Your marks, notes and choices stay in this browser tab and are cleared when you close or reset it.
